title: The Daily Loop: Stage, Commit, Inspect —

header.html: stage and commit with git add and git commit; read git status and its short codes; compare changes with git diff and git diff --staged; read history with git log and git show; remove and rename files with git rm and git mv; ignore files with .gitignore; fix the last commit with git commit --amend; write a good commit
Git 2.50.1: every command was run in the lab

toc.title: Reading changes: diff, log and show

html:
1The loop: status, add, commit

Daily work is a loop: edit files, check with git status, stage with git add, and record with git commit. The figure shows the loop. git status tells you the next command, so run it often.

git status -s is the short form. It prints two columns: the first compares the staging area with the last commit, the second compares the working tree with the staging area.

Code Meaning
?? New file that Git does not track yet
A in column one New file, staged
M in column one Modified and staged
M in column two Modified, not staged
MM Staged, then edited again
D Deleted: staged in column one, not staged in column two
R Renamed and staged
UU Unmerged conflict (module 4)
Command What it stages
git add file That file
git add . Every new, changed and deleted file here and below
git add -p Only the hunks you answer yes to, one at a time
git commit -a Edits to tracked files, then commits; new files stay out

git commit -m "message" records the staging area. Without -m, Git opens your editor for the message. Your hashes will differ from the ones in this module.

echo "cart: empty" > cart.txt
git status -s
git add cart.txt
git commit -m "Add cart"

?? cart.txt
[main (root-commit) bf6d105] Add cart
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 cart.txt
Tip

. Use git add -p to split mixed edits into separate commits. It shows each hunk and asks; answer y to stage it and n to leave it.

2Reading changes: diff, log and show

Three git diff forms answer three questions.

Command What it compares
git diff Working tree against the staging area: unstaged edits
git diff --staged Staging area against the last commit: what you will commit
git diff HEAD Working tree against the last commit: everything

--stat gives a summary and --name-only lists only the file names.

echo "cart: 2 items" > cart.txt
git diff
git add cart.txt
git status -s

diff --git a/cart.txt b/cart.txt
index f7caf72..5b24fa9 100644
--- a/cart.txt
+++ b/cart.txt
@@ -1 +1 @@
-cart: empty
+cart: 2 items
M  cart.txt

After git add, plain git diff is empty and git diff --staged shows the change.

git log lists commits, newest first. git show prints one commit with its message and patch. git show HEAD~1 shows the parent, and git show HEAD:cart.txt prints a file as it was in a commit.

Log option Effect
--oneline One line per commit
--graph --decorate --all Draw the branches and show their names
-p Add the patch of each commit
--stat Add the changed files and counts
-n 3 Only the last three commits
--author=Bob Only commits by Bob
--since="2 weeks ago" Only recent commits
-- cart.txt Only commits that touched this path 
git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all

* c461e07 (feature/search) Add search
| * 13c2b2b (HEAD -> main) Add footer
|/
* 68109f1 Update cart
* bf6d105 Add cart
Tip

. Run git diff --staged before every commit. It shows exactly what the commit will contain, so surprises stay out of history.

3Remove, rename and ignore

git rm file deletes the file and stages the deletion. git rm --cached file stops tracking a file but keeps it in your folder. git mv old new renames a file and stages the rename, and git status -s shows an R.

Moving a file by hand and then running git add gives the same result, because Git detects renames from the content.

A .gitignore file lists patterns for files Git should leave alone. Commit it, so the whole team shares the rules.

Pattern What it ignores
*.log Any file ending in .log, in any folder
build/ Any folder named build
!keep.log Exception: keep tracking this file
/todo.txt Only the todo.txt at the repository root
.git/info/exclude Personal rules for this clone, not shared

Ignore rules only affect files that are not tracked yet. A file that is already committed stays tracked, and git status keeps showing its changes. An exception also cannot reach into an ignored folder. git check-ignore -v file names the line that ignores a file.

mkdir build
touch app.log keep.log build/out.js
printf '*.log\nbuild/\n!keep.log\n' > .gitignore
git status -s
git check-ignore -v app.log

?? .gitignore
?? keep.log
.gitignore:1:*.log	app.log

Four new files exist, yet only .gitignore and keep.log are listed.

Tip

. Adding a pattern does not untrack a committed file; run git rm --cached file once. Then commit, and the rule applies from then on.

4A good commit and amend

A good commit has one logical change that you can describe in one line. The subject is in the imperative mood, as if giving an order: "Add free shipping rule", not "Added" or "Adds". Keep it to about 50 characters. If the reason is not obvious, add a blank line and a short body that says why.

Weak message Better message
fix stuff Fix cart total when a coupon is used
Updated files and added things Add free shipping rule to cart
One commit with a bug fix and a rename Two commits, one change each

git commit --amend replaces the last commit. Use -m to fix the message, or git add a forgotten file and run git commit --amend --no-edit. The result is a new commit with a new hash, and the old one is gone from the branch.

git log --oneline -n 1
git add tax.txt
git commit --amend --no-edit
git log --oneline -n 1

e9f1aa3 Add shipping rule
[main e868274] Add shipping rule
 2 files changed, 2 insertions(+)
 create mode 100644 shipping.txt
 create mode 100644 tax.txt
e868274 Add shipping rule

The message is the same, but the hash changed, so this is a new commit. The tax file joined the commit.

Tip

. Amend only commits you have not shared. Others may already have the old hash, and a changed hash causes trouble (module 6 covers the safe ways to undo).

5Practice Q&A

5.1 Practice questions (choose the best answer)

S1git status -s prints ?? notes.txt and M cart.txt. Which statement is true?

  • ABoth files are staged and ready to be committed now
  • Bnotes.txt is untracked and cart.txt has unstaged edits
  • Cnotes.txt is ignored and cart.txt is already committed
  • DBoth files have conflicts that need to be resolved
Show the answer

Answer: B. The double question mark marks a file Git does not track, and an M in the second column marks an edit that is not staged.

S2Ada staged cart.txt and then edited it again. Which command shows only the newer edit?

  • Agit diff --staged, which compares the index with the last commit
  • Bgit log -p, which prints the patches of the earlier commits
  • Cgit diff HEAD, which compares the folder with the last commit
  • Dgit diff, which compares the folder with the staging area
Show the answer

Answer: D. Plain git diff compares the working tree with the staging area, so it shows only what is not staged.

S3Cy committed debug.log by mistake, then added *.log to .gitignore. git status still shows changes to debug.log. What fixes it?

  • Agit add debug.log, which stages the file once more
  • Bgit commit -a, which saves every tracked edit at once
  • Cgit rm --cached debug.log, then commit the removal
  • Dgit check-ignore -v, which removes the file from tracking
Show the answer

Answer: C. Ignore rules do not apply to tracked files, so the file must be untracked first, and --cached keeps it in the folder.

S4Bob sees a typo in the message of his last commit. Nothing has been shared. What is the safest fix?

  • Agit commit --amend -m with the corrected message
  • Bgit reset --hard HEAD~1, then commit again from scratch
  • Cgit rm --cached on every file of the last commit
  • Dgit revert HEAD, which adds a second commit on top
Show the answer

Answer: A. Amend rewrites only the last commit, which is fine while no one else has it.

S5Ada wants the message and the patch of the commit just before the last one. Which command does it?

  • Agit diff HEAD~1, which compares the folder with that commit
  • Bgit log -n 1, which prints the message of the last commit
  • Cgit show HEAD~1, which prints the parent commit and its patch
  • Dgit status -s, which lists the files that have changes
Show the answer

Answer: C. git show prints one commit with its message and patch, and HEAD~1 names the parent of the last commit.

S6Which commit message best follows the guidance for a good commit?

  • AFixed the cart total and tidied up the shipping rules
  • BCart updates, shipping changes and a few other fixes
  • CAdding a free shipping rule to the cart total logic
  • DAdd free shipping for orders above the set threshold
Show the answer

Answer: D. It describes one change in the imperative mood and is about 50 characters, while the others are past tense, vague or mixed.

5.2 Recall questions

R1Which command shows what is staged for the next commit?

Show the answer

git diff --staged.

R2What does git add -p let you do?

Show the answer

Stage chosen hunks of a file instead of the whole file.

R3Which command renames a tracked file and stages the rename?

Show the answer

git mv old new.

R4Which command stops tracking a file but keeps it in your folder?

Show the answer

git rm --cached.

R5Which command shows the .gitignore line that ignores a file?

Show the answer

git check-ignore -v.

R6How long and in which mood should a commit subject be?

Show the answer

About 50 characters, in the imperative mood.

6Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Loop Edit, git status, git add, git commit -m, inspect
Short status ?? untracked; M modified; A added; D deleted; R renamed; two columns
Staging git add file, git add ., git add -p; git commit -a skips new files
Diff git diff unstaged; git diff --staged staged; git diff HEAD both
History git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all; -p, --stat, -n, --author, --since
Show git show for one commit; git show HEAD:file for an old file
Remove, rename git rm, git rm --cached, git mv
Ignore *.log, build/, !keep.log; tracked files are not ignored; git check-ignore -v
Good commit One change, imperative subject, about 50 characters; amend only unshared commits
